requirements.note: Edge-to-edge grid, three per row with hairline gaps, newest first, 600 tiles, symbol centred on an HSL square.
A filter button in the nav bar opens a native pull-down menu with All Boards plus 10 boards. Board name and count shown above the grid.

Pushed detail shows a large tile, title, board and date. Swiping the tile left/right moves through neighbours within the current filter (Previous is disabled on the first tile), plus Previous/Next buttons and an 'n of N' counter.
Heart in the nav bar likes and unlikes. The Liked tab uses the same grid with heart badges. Unliking from Liked removes the tile from the list.
Select turns the title into 'N Selected' and adds Cancel, Select All, check circles, and a bottom Like/Delete bar. Delete asks for confirmation in a system alert. Bulk like works.
3 deletions and the bulk likes were still there after relaunch.

bugs: After leaving select mode (after a bulk delete or like), the large 'Moodboard' title is drawn on top of the 'All Boards' header text: the content inset doesn't reset when the title returns to large.
tells: Grid tiles are exposed to accessibility as Switches rather than buttons or cells.
The detail nav title is the generic 'Tile' rather than the tile's name.
Previous/Next pill buttons and a 'Swipe the tile to explore' hint under the detail duplicate the swipe gesture. A hand-built app would rely on a paging scroll view.
The Like heart in the detail nav bar fills black instead of tinted red, while the grid badges are red.
At the largest text size the tile emoji scale with Dynamic Type until they nearly fill the tiles, and 'All Boards' wraps onto two lines.
A.scroll: A smooth system collection view: the large title collapses into an inline title with a scroll-edge blur, flings and returns to the top cleanly, no blank or popping tiles, and scroll position is kept after returning from detail.

requirements.note: Three per row, newest first, rounded tiles with 12pt margins and gaps that fill the width. Not edge-to-edge, but acceptable.
A native menu behind an 'All boards' pill button lists all 10 boards plus All boards, with a checkmark on the current one. Tile count updates.
Detail is a true horizontal paging view (swipe follows the finger) with board, serif title and 'Added <date>'. The nav title is the board name. Also has a 'n of N' bar with chevrons.
A full-width 'Like tile' button toggles to 'Liked'. The Liked tab uses the same grid with heart badges, and unliking there removes the tile.
Select mode has Select all and Cancel, check circles, a selection ring, a 'N selected' bar with Like/Delete, and a system confirmation alert. Both bulk actions work.
Deletions (597 tiles) and bulk likes were still there after relaunch, and the liked count was correct.

tells: The header (large title, tagline, filter pill, count) is pinned outside the grid's scroll view, so the large title never collapses and the grid scrolls in a clipped window under a fixed header. Only about 2/3 of the screen shows tiles, and less than half at the largest text size.
Custom branding (red accent, serif detail title, tagline 'A little inspiration, collected.') reads more like a designed web or React page than a stock iOS app.
At the largest text size the detail's 'Added October…' date runs under the bottom 'n of N' bar, which overlaps the content.
A heavy full-width filled 'Like tile' button where iOS would put a nav-bar or toolbar heart.
B.scroll: Flings smoothly with no blank or popping tiles, and scroll position is kept after returning from detail. But the grid scrolls inside a box under a fixed header, so the large title never collapses and there is no scroll-edge effect, which doesn't feel like an iPhone list.

why: Both apps meet all six requirements and persist correctly. A behaves more like a native iOS app: edge-to-edge grid, a large title that collapses on scroll, filter in the nav bar. B has a nicer paging detail view and no functional bugs, but its fixed, non-collapsing header takes up a third of the screen on every scroll, which an iOS user notices right away. A's title-overlap glitch after select mode is a real flaw, but a transient one, so A edges ahead.
